pos: n. (a clasp or catch; rendering Hebrew qeres)
etymology: From Old French tache, a fastening; the same root gives us attach. In the English Bible the word lives almost entirely in the tabernacle chapters of Exodus.
biblical_def: A tache is a clasp of gold or brass by which the curtains of the tabernacle were coupled into one tent. Fifty taches of gold joined the inner curtains, and fifty of brass the outer covering, “that it may be one tabernacle” (Exo 26:6). The word carries a small doctrine: the dwelling of God is not a heap of parts but one whole, and the joints that make it one are named and counted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tache as something used for taking hold or holding; a catch; a loop; a button — citing this very use in Exodus.
webster_full: TACHE, n. Something used for taking hold or holding; a catch; a loop; a button.
scriptures: Exo 26:6
And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle.
And thou shalt make fifty taches of brass, and put the taches into the loops, and couple the tent together, that it may be one.

And thou shalt hang up the vail under the taches, that thou mayest bring in thither within the vail the ark of the testimony: and the vail shall divide unto you between the holy place and the most holy.
The tabernacle, his tent, and his covering, his taches, and his boards, his bars, his pillars, and his sockets,
corruption_summary: Modern versions replace taches with clasps, which is accurate and loses nothing except the reminder that readers once knew tabernacle hardware by name.
corruption_paragraphs: The loss here is not doctrinal but devotional. Generations of English readers slowed down over the taches, the loops, the sockets, and the boards, and learned that God cared to specify how His dwelling was joined together. A church that skims the tabernacle chapters as tedious inventory misses what the taches teach — that the unity of the one tent hung, literally, on small unglamorous fastenings.

The veil hung “under the taches” (Exo 26:33), placing the boundary between the holy place and the most holy at the very seam of the tent. The geography of access to God was built into the hardware — until the veil was rent from top to bottom, and the seam opened.
roots_summary: Hebrew qeres (H7165), a hook or clasp, occurs only in the tabernacle narratives of Exodus.
roots_lines: Hebrew qeres (H7165) — hook, clasp; the coupling hardware of the tabernacle curtains, ten occurrences, all in Exodus 26–39.
usage: “And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold” — the joints of God's dwelling are specified, not improvised.
“Couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle” — unity by design.
“Thou shalt hang up the vail under the taches” — the boundary of the holiest hung at the seam.

pos: n. (a veil or hood; rendering Hebrew mitpachath)
etymology: From Old English wimpel, a head-covering wound about the neck and chin; the garment survives in paintings of medieval nuns. The KJV uses it once, in Isaiah's inventory of Zion's finery.
biblical_def: A wimple is an ample veil or shawl wound about the head. It appears in Isaiah 3, where the LORD strips the daughters of Zion of every article of pride — “the changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins” (Isa 3:22). The catalogue is deliberately exhaustive: when judgment comes for pride, nothing in the wardrobe is exempt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wimple as a hood or veil, citing Isaiah 3, and notes the verb sense, to draw down as a veil.
webster_full: WIMPLE, n. A hood or veil. Is. 3.
scriptures: Isa 3:22
The changeable suits of apparel, and the mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins,
Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
corruption_summary: Modern versions render the word cloaks or shawls; the item is minor, but the sermon of Isaiah 3 — that God audits wardrobes when they become altars — is widely unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 3 is one of the most specific judgment passages in Scripture, and its specificity is the point. The prophet does not condemn adornment in the abstract; he lists twenty-one items, wimples among them, worn by women “with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes” (Isa 3:16). It is the haughtiness, not the fabric, that draws the sentence — but the sentence falls on the fabric, because pride had made the fabric its banner.

The apostolic counterweight is not frumpiness but a transferred adornment: “whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning… but let it be the hidden man of the heart” (1Pe 3:3–4). The wimple itself was never the problem. A wardrobe becomes an idol only when the wearer does.
roots_summary: Hebrew mitpachath (H4304), a wide cloak or shawl; elsewhere it is the “vail” of Ruth that carried six measures of barley.
roots_lines: Hebrew mitpachath (H4304) — shawl, wide wrap; Isaiah's wimples and Ruth's vail (Ruth 3:15) are the same garment.
usage: “The mantles, and the wimples, and the crisping pins” — judgment reads the wardrobe line by line.
“Because the daughters of Zion are haughty” — the charge is pride; the finery is evidence.
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain” — the proverb the wimple list preaches.

pos: n. (an embassy, a delegation; rendering Greek presbeia)
etymology: An older form of embassage or embassy, from the same root as ambassador. The KJV uses it in our Lord's parable of the king counting the cost of war.
biblical_def: An ambassage is a delegation sent to negotiate. In Luke 14:32 a king who cannot match an approaching army “sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.” Christ places the picture inside His teaching on discipleship: count the cost, for you cannot meet God in battle. The ambassage is the sinner's only sane diplomacy — sue for peace while the King is yet a great way off.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats embassage and ambassage as the message or public function of an ambassador; the older spelling was already fading in his day.
webster_full: AMBASSAGE, n. The message or business of an ambassador; an embassy. [Little used.] Luke 14.
scriptures: Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?
Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
Isa 27:5
Or let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me; and he shall make peace with me.
corruption_summary: Modern renderings say delegation, which is clear enough; what is corrupted is the parable's application, softened from surrender before God into a lesson about planning.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable is often preached as prudent project management — count your resources before you commit. But the king with ten thousand facing twenty thousand is not a lesson in logistics; he is every sinner measuring himself against the holiness of God and discovering the arithmetic is hopeless. The ambassage is not a stratagem. It is capitulation dressed in diplomacy, and Christ commends it.

The gospel then reverses the direction of the embassy. Having taught sinners to sue for peace, God Himself dispatches the delegation: “we are ambassadors for Christ… be ye reconciled to God” (2Co 5:20). The offended King sends His own ambassage to the rebels — terms of peace purchased at the cross, offered before the army arrives.
roots_summary: Greek presbeia (G4242), an embassy or body of elders sent with authority; cognate with presbeuo, to act as ambassador (2Co 5:20).
roots_lines: Greek presbeia (G4242) — embassy, delegation; Luke 14:32 and Luke 19:14.
Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to be an ambassador; Paul's word for the ministry of reconciliation.
usage: “He sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace” — surrender is the only sane diplomacy with God.
“Or else, while the other is yet a great way off” — the time to seek terms is before the battle.
“Let him take hold of my strength, that he may make peace with me” — the terms are already published.

etymology: From the old verb neese, to sneeze — the ancestor of our modern word. The KJV keeps it in one of the most untamed passages in the Bible, the LORD's description of leviathan.
biblical_def: Neesings are sneezes. “By his neesings a light doth shine, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning” (Job 41:18) — leviathan's very snorting flashes light. The word sits in God's closing argument to Job: a creature so wild that its sneeze is dreadful was made, and is mastered, by the LORD alone. If the creature's neesing is beyond man, what is the Creator?
webster_summary: Webster (1828) records neese, to sneeze, as retained from the older English Bibles, and neesing as the act of sneezing.
webster_full: NEESE, v.i. To sneeze. [This orthography is retained in our Bibles.] 2 Kings 4.
NEESING, n. A sneezing. Job 41.
scriptures: By his neesings a light doth shine, and his eyes are like the eyelids of the morning.
None is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?
Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes. to and
Job 42:2
I know that thou canst do every thing, and that no thought can be withholden from thee.
corruption_summary: Modern versions print sneezings, which is faithful; the deeper loss is a doctrine of creation tamed into nature documentary, where leviathan becomes a crocodile and the argument loses its terror.
corruption_paragraphs: The rhetorical weight of Job 41 depends on the creature being genuinely beyond human mastery. When commentators reduce leviathan to a large reptile with poetic exaggeration, the LORD's question — “none is so fierce that dare stir him up: who then is able to stand before me?” (Job 41:10) — deflates into a zoology lesson. The neesings that flash light are meant to overwhelm, not to be explained.

The other biblical sneeze belongs to the Shunammite's son, who “sneezed seven times, and opened his eyes” (2Ki 4:35) under Elisha's ministry. Between leviathan's dreadful neesings and a dead boy's reviving ones stands the same truth: breath, violent or gentle, is the LORD's to give.
roots_summary: Hebrew atishah (H5846), sneezing, occurs only in Job 41:18; the verb behind the Shunammite boy's sneezing (2Ki 4:35) is zarar (H2237).
roots_lines: Hebrew atishah (H5846) — a sneeze; only of leviathan, Job 41:18.
Hebrew zarar (H2237) — to sneeze; the revived child of 2 Kings 4:35.
usage: “By his neesings a light doth shine” — even the beast's reflex is beyond man's imitation.
“Who then is able to stand before me?” — the argument the neesing serves.
“The child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes” — breath returns at the LORD's word.

etymology: From Old English hoh, the hollow behind the knee — pronounced hock, as in the hock of a horse. To hough is to cut the great tendon there, disabling the animal without killing it.
biblical_def: To hough is to hamstring. The LORD commanded Joshua concerning the northern kings' cavalry: “thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots with fire” (Jos 11:6). Israel was forbidden to absorb the enemy's war machine into her own army; the instruments of confidence in flesh were to be disabled, not redeployed. David did the same with the chariot horses of Zobah (2Sa 8:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives hough as the joint of the hind leg, and the verb, to hamstring; to disable by cutting the sinews of the ham.
webster_full: HOUGH, n. hok. The lower part of the thigh; the ham; the joint of the hind leg of a beast that connects the thigh with the leg.
HOUGH, v.t. hok. To hamstring; to disable by cutting the sinews of the ham. Josh. 11.
scriptures: Jos 11:6

And the LORD said unto Joshua, Be not afraid because of them: for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel: thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots with fire.
Jos 11:9
And Joshua did unto them as the LORD bade him: he houghed their horses, and burnt their chariots with fire.
And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: and David houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them for an hundred chariots.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Modern versions translate hamstring, accurately; what the church corrupts is the principle — captured strength is routinely enlisted rather than houghed, and ministries ride the very horses God said to disable.
corruption_paragraphs: The command offends military sense. Captured cavalry was the ancient world's greatest prize, and Israel was ordered to ruin it. The reason is stated elsewhere: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). A church that wins some cultural battle and immediately adopts the enemy's machinery of influence has kept the horses — and will soon trust them.

The kings of Israel were expressly forbidden to multiply horses (Deu 17:16), and Solomon's stables measure his drift. Houghing is the discipline of refusing strength that would relocate your confidence. It looks like waste. It is worship.
roots_summary: Hebrew aqar (H6131), to pluck up or hamstring; the same root describes rooting up, which is what houghing does to an army's power.
roots_lines: Hebrew aqar (H6131) — to pluck up by the roots; to hamstring; Joshua 11:6, 9 and 2 Samuel 8:4.
Genesis 49:6 uses the same verb of Simeon and Levi, who “digged down a wall” — margin, houghed oxen — in their anger.
usage: “Thou shalt hough their horses, and burn their chariots” — enemy strength is disabled, not enlisted.
“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” — the trust the command protects against.
“He shall not multiply horses to himself” — the king's copy of the same discipline.

pos: v. part. (paneled, wainscoted; rendering Hebrew saphan and chaphah)
etymology: The old spelling of ceiled, from a root meaning to cover or overlay — whence our word ceiling. In Scripture the covering is usually costly cedar or fir paneling.
biblical_def: To be cieled is to be lined with fine paneling. Haggai turns the word into an indictment: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The greater house of the temple was cieled with fir and gold (2Ch 3:5); the scandal of Haggai's generation was private luxury financed by sanctuary neglect. Jeremiah adds the matching woe on the king who builds wide chambers “cieled with cedar” by unrighteousness (Jer 22:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ciel as to overlay or cover the inner roof of a building, and cieled as overlaid with a ceiling — citing 2 Chronicles 3.
webster_full: CIELED, pp. Overlaid with a ceiling. 2 Chron. 3.
CIEL, v.t. To overlay or cover the inner roof of a building; to make a ceiling.
scriptures: Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains.
That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion.
Hag 1:7
Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Consider your ways.
corruption_summary: Modern versions read paneled houses, and the sting survives translation; what the church corrupts is the audit itself, having learned to call sanctuary-starving comfort by the name of stewardship.
corruption_paragraphs: Haggai's question is a comparison of ceilings. The people's houses were finished to the last panel while the LORD's house lay in rubble, and the prophet's remedy is not guilt but attention: “Consider your ways” (Hag 1:7). The cieled house is not condemned for its cedar — the temple itself was cieled — but for the waste next door that funded it.

Jeremiah's woe lands on Jehoiakim, who cieled his chambers with cedar while paying no wages (Jer 22:13–14), and the verdict redefines royalty: “he judged the cause of the poor and needy… was not this to know me? saith the LORD” (Jer 22:16). Paneling is honest wealth or plundered wages depending on what it cost the neighbour — and God reads the invoice.
roots_summary: Hebrew saphan (H5603), to cover or panel, gives Haggai and Jeremiah their cieled houses; chaphah (H2645), to overlay, ciels the temple with fir.
roots_lines: Hebrew saphan (H5603) — to cover, to panel; Haggai 1:4, Jeremiah 22:14, and the king's house of cedar in 1 Kings 7:3.
Hebrew chaphah (H2645) — to overlay; the greater house cieled with fir and fine gold, 2 Chronicles 3:5.
usage: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses?” — the prophet audits the ceilings.
“And this house lie waste” — the comparison that convicts.
“That saith, I will build me a wide house… cieled with cedar” — luxury by unpaid wages is woe, not stewardship.

pos: v. (endureth, lasteth; rendering Greek proskairos, for a season)
etymology: From the old verb dure, to last — the root that survives in endure, durable, and duration. The KJV keeps the bare verb once, in the parable of the sower.
biblical_def: Dureth means lasts. The stony-ground hearer “heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it; yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while” (Mat 13:20–21). The word measures the exact tragedy of shallow conversion: real joy, real reception, real duration — for a while. What has no root does not die instantly; it dureth, then withers when the sun of tribulation rises.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dure as to last, to hold on in time, to endure — marking it already obsolete outside the biblical text.
webster_full: DURE, v.i. [L. duro.] To last; to hold on in time or being; to continue; to endure. [Obsolete.] Matt. 13.
scriptures: But he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;
Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.
Joh 8:31
Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed;
Col 2:7
Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith, as ye have been taught, abounding therein with thanksgiving.
corruption_summary: Modern versions say endures for a while, keeping the sense; the corruption is pastoral — evangelism that counts the anon-with-joy moment as the harvest, and never waits to see what dureth.
corruption_paragraphs: The stony-ground hearer is the most deceiving figure in the parable because everything visible is right: hearing, immediacy, joy. Only time exposes him. A church that measures conversion by the response card has adopted a metric the parable was designed to discredit — Christ's own metric is root, and root is proven by what dureth through tribulation.

The remedy is not suspicion of joy but the ministry of rooting: “Rooted and built up in him, and stablished in the faith” (Col 2:7). Perseverance is not the convert's unaided grip; it is the fruit of union with Christ — and the proof, as our Lord said, is continuing: “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” (Joh 8:31).
roots_summary: Greek proskairos (G4340), for a season, temporary — the stony hearer dureth pros kairon, until the season turns.
roots_lines: Greek proskairos (G4340) — lasting for a season; the stony hearer (Mat 13:21), the pleasures of sin (Heb 11:25), and the things which are seen (2Co 4:18) all share this word.
usage: “Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while” — duration without root has a deadline.
“When tribulation or persecution ariseth… by and by he is offended” — the sun that tests the soil.
“If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed” — the metric Christ actually uses.

pos: n. (a snare, a trap; rendering Hebrew moqesh and pach)
etymology: A contraction of engine — any contrived device; in the English Bible always a contrivance for catching. The cotton gin preserves the same shortening.
biblical_def: A gin is a set trap. Job's friend describes the wicked man's path: “the gin shall take him by the heel” (Job 18:9); Amos asks whether a bird falls in a snare where no gin is laid for him (Amo 3:5). Most solemnly, Isaiah says the LORD of hosts Himself shall be “for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isa 8:14) — the same God who is a sanctuary to those who fear Him is a trap to those who stumble at Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gin as a machine or instrument — a contraction of engine — and specifically a trap or snare.
webster_full: GIN, n. [A contraction of engine.] A machine or instrument by which the mechanical powers are employed in aid of human strength.
2. An instrument for catching; a trap; a snare. Job 18. Is. 8.
scriptures: Job 18:9
The gin shall take him by the heel, and the robber shall prevail against him.
Isa 8:14
And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
Amo 3:5
Can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth, where no gin is for him? shall one take up a snare from the earth, and have taken nothing at all?
Keep me from the snares which they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity.
corruption_summary: Modern versions say trap, which is exact; what is corrupted is Isaiah's hard doctrine — a Christ who can only ever be refuge, never a stone of stumbling and a gin.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 8:14 is quoted by both Peter and Paul, and neither softens it: the same Lord is sanctuary or snare depending on the man. Preaching that offers Christ as unconditional comfort with no possibility of stumbling has filed the teeth off the gin — but the apostles kept them: “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word” (1Pe 2:8).

The believer's prayer meanwhile treats gins as a live hazard of the road: “Keep me from the snares which they have laid for me, and the gins of the workers of iniquity” (Psa 141:9). The mature saint walks like a man in trapped country — not in terror, but not carelessly; deliverance from the fowler's snare is covenant mercy, not a metaphor outgrown.
roots_summary: Hebrew moqesh (H4170), a snare or bait-stick, and pach (H6341), a spring-net; the pair appear together when the LORD Himself is the gin and the snare.
roots_lines: Hebrew moqesh (H4170) — snare, lure; the gin of Job 18:9 and Amos 3:5.
Hebrew pach (H6341) — a spring trap or net; paired with moqesh in Isaiah 8:14 and Psalm 141:9.
usage: “The gin shall take him by the heel” — the wicked man's road is trapped country.
“He shall be… for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” — the sanctuary Himself, refused, becomes the trap.
“Keep me from the snares which they have laid for me” — the saint prays like a man who believes in gins.

etymology: Past tense of hoise, the older form of hoist — a seaman's word for raising sail. It survives in Shakespeare's “hoist with his own petard” and in one verse of Acts.
biblical_def: Hoised means hoisted. In the wreck narrative of Acts 27 the sailors, having cut the anchors, “hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” (Act 27:40). The word marks the moment of committed action in one of Scripture's great providence stories: every human skill is spent — anchors, rudder bands, sail — and every life is saved exactly as God had told Paul beforehand.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives hoise as to lift or raise, especially aboard ship — noting hoist as the form that displaced it.
webster_full: HOISE, v.t. To lift; to raise; to heave; particularly, to raise by means of tackle, as a sail. [Now written hoist.] Acts 27.
scriptures: And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore.
And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship.
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
corruption_summary: Modern versions say hoisted; nothing is lost in the word, but the chapter's doctrine — absolute promise working through ordinary seamanship — is regularly split into either fatalism or self-help.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 27 holds together what the church keeps pulling apart. God promises categorically that no life shall be lost (Act 27:22–24); Paul then insists with equal force that “except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” (Act 27:31). The promise does not make the sailors idle, and the seamanship does not make the promise conditional. The hoised mainsail is means inside decree.

Fatalism cuts the sail loose — if God has promised, why labour? Self-reliance cuts the promise loose — it was good sailing that beached the ship. Luke's narrative refuses both: they hoised the sail because God had promised, and all came safe to land because they hoised the sail. That is how providence ordinarily works, at sea and in salvation history.
roots_summary: Greek epairo (G1869), to lift up — the word used of hoisting the sail, of lifting up eyes and voices, and of the Lord's ascension.
roots_lines: Greek epairo (G1869) — to lift, raise; the mainsail of Acts 27:40, the lifted eyes of Luke 18:13, and the Lord taken up in Acts 1:9.
usage: “They… hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” — means inside decree.
“There shall be no loss of any man's life among you” — the promise the sail served.
“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the necessity the promise employed.

etymology: Frequentative of scrape — to scratch about with the hands. The KJV uses it once, of David's feigned madness at the gate of Gath.
biblical_def: To scrabble is to scratch and paw. Fleeing Saul into Philistine territory, David was recognized, “and he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1Sa 21:13). The anointed of the LORD, clawing at a gate with drool in his beard — Scripture does not launder its heroes. Out of that humiliation came two psalms of trust, Psalm 34 and Psalm 56.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines scrabble as to scrape, paw or scratch with the hands, citing this verse; the word is the parent of scribble's rougher cousin.
webster_full: SCRABBLE, v.i. To scrape, paw or scratch with the hands; to move along on the hands and knees by clawing with the hands. 1 Sam. 21.
2. To make irregular or crooked marks; as, children scrabble when they begin to write.
scriptures: And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard.
Psa 34:4
I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
Psa 56:3
What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Modern versions say made marks on the doors; the picture survives, but hagiography corrupts the lesson — a David too dignified to scrabble teaches a faith too polished to be real.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 34 carries the superscription tying it to this very episode — when he changed his behaviour before Abimelech — and its content is startling for it: “I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears” (Psa 34:4). David does not edit the scrabbling out of his testimony. The psalm of radiant trust was written by the man with spittle in his beard, and the honesty is the doctrine.

The episode also disciplines how the church tells its stories. A movement that presents its leaders only in strength produces disciples who conclude their own fear disqualifies them. “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee” (Psa 56:3) was written in Gath — fear and faith in the same breath, strength made perfect in weakness.
roots_summary: Hebrew tavah (H8427), to make a mark — the same root marks the foreheads of the mourners in Ezekiel 9:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew tavah (H8427) — to make a mark, to scrabble; David's marks on the gate of Gath (1Sa 21:13) and the mark set upon the foreheads in Ezekiel 9:4.
usage: “And scrabbled on the doors of the gate” — the anointed king at his lowest, unedited.
“This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him” — Psalm 34's verdict on the Gath episode.
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee” — written by the man who scrabbled.

pos: n. (a piece of silver; rendering Hebrew keseph)
etymology: Silver with the diminutive -ling — a little silver, a silver coin. The KJV coins the word once, in Isaiah's vineyard judgment.
biblical_def: A silverling is a silver piece. Isaiah pictures the day when “every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings, it shall even be for briers and thorns” (Isa 7:23). A vineyard whose vines were each worth a silverling — premium stock, valued to the coin — reverts to wilderness under judgment. The word prices the loss: what men had appraised so carefully, unbelief forfeits entirely.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) records silverling as a silver coin, citing Isaiah — a word the Bible gave English and English barely used again.
webster_full: SILVERLING, n. A silver coin. Is. 7.
scriptures: Isa 7:23
And it shall come to pass in that day, that every place shall be, where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings, it shall even be for briers and thorns.
Isa 5:6
And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
Hag 2:8
The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Modern versions read shekels of silver; the accounting survives, but the sermon — that judgment devalues what markets prized — is rarely carried to the ledger it targets.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's arithmetic is deliberate: a thousand vines at a thousand silverlings is a valuation, the kind men quote with pride. The judgment does not merely damage the vineyard; it deletes the price column. Briers and thorns have no unit value. Every culture that measures its vineyards only in silverlings is one visitation away from discovering what its portfolio is worth before God.

Silver runs through Scripture as the metal of purchase and betrayal — Joseph sold for twenty pieces, the Lord appraised at thirty (Mat 26:15). Against every market stands one declaration: “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts” (Hag 2:8). The silverlings were always His; the vines too.
roots_summary: Hebrew keseph (H3701), silver, money — in Isaiah 7:23 counted per vine; the word doubles for currency throughout the Old Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew keseph (H3701) — silver, money; a thousand silverlings per thousand vines (Isa 7:23), and the thirty pieces weighed for the Shepherd (Zec 11:12).
usage: “A thousand vines at a thousand silverlings” — the market's careful appraisal, on the eve of briers.
“It shall even be for briers and thorns” — judgment deletes the price column.
“The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD” — the true ledger.

etymology: From Latin tilia, the lime or linden tree. The KJV chose it once, for the great terebinth of Isaiah's call vision.
biblical_def: The teil tree stands in Isaiah 6:13, the verse that closes the prophet's commission. Israel will be felled by judgment, “as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.” The teil can be cut to a stump and live; the life is in the root, not the foliage. So the nation: devastated to a stump, yet holding the holy seed — the remnant, and in the end the Messiah — as its substance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) identifies the teil as the lime or linden tree, the KJV's rendering of the great long-lived tree of Isaiah 6:13.
webster_full: TEIL, n. [L. tilia.] The lime tree, otherwise called the linden. Is. 6.
scriptures: Isa 6:13

But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.
Isa 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
Job 14:7
For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease.
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
corruption_summary: Modern versions read terebinth, the likelier tree; the botany improves while the doctrine of the stump — judgment that preserves a living remnant — goes unpreached in churches embarrassed by judgment altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's commission is among the darkest in Scripture — preach until the cities be wasted — and verse 13 is its single shaft of light. The tree is felled, but felled like a teil: “there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again” (Job 14:7). Judgment in the hands of God is never annihilation of the elect; the stump is a nursery.

From that stump the promise sharpens to a point: “there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isa 11:1). The holy seed in the stump of the teil is first the remnant according to the election of grace (Rom 11:5), and finally Christ Himself — the shoot that outlives the axe.
roots_summary: Hebrew elah (H424), the terebinth — a tree that regrows from its stump; elsewhere it shades Gideon and catches Absalom.
roots_lines: Hebrew elah (H424) — terebinth, great tree; the teil of Isaiah 6:13, Gideon's oak at Ophrah (Jdg 6:11), and the oak that held Absalom (2Sa 18:9).
usage: “As a teil tree… whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves” — life in the root survives the felling.
“So the holy seed shall be the substance thereof” — the stump is a nursery, not a grave.
“There shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse” — the Shoot the stump was keeping.

etymology: Literally not-toward — not facing the right way; froward's cousin. A generation that will not point toward God is untoward.
biblical_def: Untoward means crooked, bent away. It is Peter's word at Pentecost: “Save yourselves from this untoward generation” (Act 2:40). The Greek is skolios — the crooked of “the crooked shall be made straight” — and Peter's exhortation assumes a generation can have a shape, a collective bend away from God strong enough that salvation includes separation from it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines untoward as froward, perverse, refractory — also awkward and ungraceful — the moral sense leading.
webster_full: UNTOWARD, a. Froward; perverse; refractory; not easily guided or taught. Acts 2.
2. Awkward; ungraceful.
3. Inconvenient; troublesome; unmanageable.
scriptures: Act 2:40
And with many other words did he testify and exhort, saying, Save yourselves from this untoward generation.
Php 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world;
Deu 32:5
They have corrupted themselves, their spot is not the spot of his children: they are a perverse and crooked generation. They
Luk 3:5
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth;
corruption_summary: Modern versions read corrupt or crooked generation, keeping the force; the corruption is the church's embarrassment at the exhortation itself — evangelism that invites men to Christ without calling them out of anything.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's Pentecost appeal is the pattern of apostolic evangelism, and its final note is separation: be saved from this untoward generation. The generation is not a demographic insult; it is Moses' old diagnosis — “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deu 32:5) — renewed on the men who had just crucified their Messiah. A gospel that adds Christ to a life still pointed the old way has not preached Peter's sermon.

The saved are then set back among the untoward as light: “blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world” (Php 2:15). Separation is moral, not monastic — pulled out of the generation's bend, planted back in its midst, pointed toward God.
roots_summary: Greek skolios (G4646), crooked, bent — the untoward generation of Acts 2, the crooked nation of Philippians 2, and the crooked ways made straight before the Lord.
roots_lines: Greek skolios (G4646) — crooked, perverse; Acts 2:40, Philippians 2:15, 1 Peter 2:18 (froward masters), and the crooked made straight in Luke 3:5.
usage: “Save yourselves from this untoward generation” — salvation includes a direction, out and away.
“A perverse and crooked generation” — Moses' diagnosis, renewed at Pentecost.
“In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights” — separated in bent, returned in witness.
